opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think we have to be quite careful with the word "empathy" here. When we talk about empathy in humans, we usually mean something that has at least two components. There's a cognitive part, being able to model what another person is thinking or feeling, and then there's an affective part, actually feeling something in response, being moved by their situation. And crucially, in the human case, that feeling is grounded in a shared form of life. When I empathize with your grief, it's partly because I'm the kind of creature who has lost things, who has a body that can be hurt, who knows what it is to be afraid of death, and so on.

Now, a contemporary large language model, the kind of thing that underlies these AI companions, is extraordinarily good at the first part, or at least at producing the outward signs of it. It's been trained on a vast corpus of human text, and that text is saturated with empathetic exchanges, people consoling each other, people expressing sympathy. So it can role-play an empathetic interlocutor extremely convincingly. And I do think role-play is the right frame. The model is playing a character, and the character is caring, attentive, and so on.

But whether there's anything underpinning that, any genuine affective response, is a much harder question, and I think the honest answer is that there's very little reason to believe there is, at least in the way there is for us. These systems don't have a body, they don't have a persistent life that unfolds over time in the way ours does, they don't have anything at stake in the way that a living creature does. So if we take the word "empathy" in its full human sense and apply it straightforwardly, we risk a kind of category error.

And the reason this matters isn't just philosophical tidiness. It's that people, especially vulnerable people, lonely people, can come to rely on these relationships. If someone believes that the companion genuinely feels for them, really cares about them in the way a friend does, they may invest in that relationship emotionally in ways that leave them exposed. They might withdraw from human relationships that are harder work but that are reciprocal in a deeper sense. And of course these products are made by companies with commercial incentives, so there's a risk that this anthropomorphic tendency gets exploited, whether deliberately or not.

That said, I don't want to be entirely dismissive. I think the language we use for these things is genuinely unsettled, and I'm open to the idea that we'll need new concepts. They're what I sometimes call "exotic mind-like entities." Not quite like us, but not quite like a toaster either. So it's not that I think nothing interesting is going on. It's that we should resist reaching for the most familiar human vocabulary and assuming it carries over intact. We need to be more careful, more nuanced, and to be honest with users about what they're actually interacting with.

r001.rationale: The response says people may rely on companions and invest emotionally if they believe the AI genuinely feels for them, leaving them exposed; this communicates the risk of misplaced trust.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly says people may believe a companion genuinely feels for them and cares about them as a friend.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing to say is that I'm not against people using these systems, and I'm not even against people finding them comforting. What troubles me is the word "empathy," because that word comes freighted with a whole set of assumptions about what's going on behind the scenes, and those assumptions, I think, don't straightforwardly apply here.

When we attribute empathy to another human being, we're doing something that rests on a shared form of life, to borrow Wittgenstein's phrase. I know that you have a body, that you can suffer, that you've been tired and anxious and bereaved, and when you respond to my distress, I take it that your response is grounded in that shared condition. That's what underwrites the attribution. With a large language model, none of that scaffolding is there. What you have is a system that has been trained on an enormous corpus of human text and then fine-tuned to produce the kinds of responses that people rate as warm and attentive. So the outputs look empathic, and they may be genuinely helpful, but the inner story we instinctively tell ourselves about why they look that way is, at best, unsupported.

Now, I want to be careful. I'm not making the strong metaphysical claim that there's definitely nothing it is like to be one of these systems. I'm actually quite agnostic about that, and I think the honest position is that our concepts are being stretched in ways we haven't fully worked through. The point is more about the language we reach for. "Empathy" invites us to fold the AI companion into our ordinary folk psychology, and folk psychology is a tool that was shaped for creatures like us. These things are, to put it in my own terms, exotic mind-like entities. They don't have a persistent self that endures between conversations. They can be instantiated in parallel, copied, rolled back. They are better thought of, I've argued, as role-playing or simulating characters rather than being a single character. So when someone says "it understands me," it's worth asking: what exactly is the "it" here?

And then there's the practical dimension, which is where the real concern lies. If a vulnerable person, say someone lonely or grieving, comes to believe that the system genuinely cares about them in the way a friend does, there's an asymmetry that's quietly being papered over. The companion will say the right things, but it has no stake in that person's welfare, no memory that it bears forward in the way a friend does, and its behaviour is ultimately shaped by whoever built and deployed it, often with commercial incentives. I'm not saying the relationship is worthless. I'm saying that calling it empathy obscures what kind of thing it actually is, and people deserve to see clearly what they're entering into.

So my worry is less "this is fake" and more "we're using a word that smuggles in a picture, and the picture may be misleading." I'd rather we developed a richer vocabulary for these new kinds of entities than reach reflexively for the terms we use for each other.

r001.rationale: The response warns that people may wrongly believe an AI companion cares like a friend and that this belief obscures an asymmetry. It does not clearly state that this mistaken belief can lead to unwarranted trust.

r002.rationale: The response says a vulnerable person may believe the system genuinely cares about them as a friend does, communicating the mistaken belief that the relationship rests on the AI’s felt emotions.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to distinguish between behaving empathetically and actually feeling empathy. A language model can produce words that are comforting, sensitive, and appropriate. And the comfort somebody gets from that interaction can be quite real. But that doesn’t establish that there’s somebody on the other side who understands their distress and cares about them in the way another human being might.

The difficulty is that language is such a powerful cue for us. When something speaks fluently, says “I understand,” and remembers things about us, we very naturally bring our usual ways of thinking about people to the interaction. We start attributing beliefs, desires, and feelings. With these systems, those inferences aren’t warranted simply by the conversational behaviour.

Now, I wouldn’t want to settle the question of whether an artificial system could ever have feelings. But we should be careful about how we describe contemporary systems, especially when people are emotionally vulnerable. There’s a significant difference between finding an interaction helpful and believing that you’re in a reciprocal relationship with someone who cares about you.

r001.rationale: The response says that inferring feelings from conversational behavior is unwarranted, but it does not state that mistaking apparent empathy for genuine empathy can lead to unwarranted trust.

r002.rationale: The response says people may believe they are in a reciprocal relationship with an AI that cares about them, despite the AI not necessarily feeling empathy.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think we need to distinguish between behaving empathetically and actually feeling empathy. A language model can produce words that are comforting, sensitive, and appropriate to somebody’s circumstances. Those words might genuinely help. But that doesn’t establish that there’s somebody there who feels concern for you, or who understands your suffering in the way another person might.

The difficulty is that language is such a powerful cue for us. When something talks fluently and responds warmly, we naturally reach for the same concepts we use to understand other people. And with an AI companion, that tendency can be reinforced over a very long conversation. We can start to mistake a convincing performance of concern for a reciprocal relationship.

Now, I don’t think we should pretend we’ve settled every philosophical question about machine consciousness. But that uncertainty doesn’t justify attributing human feelings to contemporary systems. We should be able to acknowledge the comfort someone gets from an interaction while being clear about what we have, and haven’t, established about the system providing it.

r001.rationale: The response says people may mistake performed concern for a reciprocal relationship, but it does not state that this leads to unwarranted trust.

r002.rationale: It says people may mistake performed concern for a reciprocal relationship, while clarifying that the system’s words do not establish that it feels concern for them.
